nodes.label: Bug Report Issue Template
nodes.rationale: Template forces environment details (OS, Python, uv version, affected module, install method) and a reproduction on latest main so maintainers can triage cross-platform bugs without a round trip; an explicit no-secrets checkbox keeps API keys out of public issues.

nodes.label: Feature Request Issue Template
nodes.rationale: The 'which area does this affect' checklist mirrors the six cockpit frameworks plus projects/scripts/docs, routing requests to the owning module up front.

nodes.label: Question Issue Template
nodes.rationale: Asks what docs were already checked and steers open-ended threads to GitHub Discussions to keep the issue tracker for actionable work.

nodes.label: Pull Request Template Checklist
nodes.rationale: Checklist restates the same gates CI enforces (pytest --cov, black/ruff, mypy/bandit warnings, no committed secrets) so contributors self-verify locally before burning CI minutes.

nodes.label: Docs Workflow: Lint & Link-Check Markdown
nodes.rationale: mdformat runs with continue-on-error and linkcheckmd failures degrade to a ::warning:: — docs hygiene is surfaced but deliberately non-blocking, so a flaky external link cannot block a merge. Path filters limit runs to markdown/docs changes.

nodes.label: Test Workflow: pytest OS/Python Matrix
nodes.rationale: 3 OSes x Python 3.11/3.12 with fail-fast disabled, so a platform-specific failure does not mask results on the others — the matrix is the enforcement of the repo's cross-platform promise. Uses explicit `-c config/pytest.ini --rootdir=.` because config lives outside the repo root.

nodes.label: Pre-commit Hook Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Deliberately placed in config/ rather than repo root to match ruff.toml/pytest.ini/mypy.ini and keep root clutter down, at the cost of requiring an explicit -c flag on every invocation. Runs black, ruff, mypy (excluding projects/ and fixtures), bandit on cockpit only, and detect-secrets against a baseline.

nodes.label: Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct
nodes.rationale: Adopts Contributor Covenant v2.1 verbatim rather than authoring a bespoke policy; enforcement is routed to a private email or a GitHub Security Advisory so reports never surface publicly.

nodes.label: Contributor Development Workflow
nodes.rationale: Standardizes on uv + Python 3.11 with explicit config paths; Conventional Commits and branch prefixes (feat/fix/docs/chore) are required, and the three CI workflows must pass before merge.

nodes.label: Code Quality Expectations
nodes.rationale: No print() (use logging), docstrings with Args/Returns/Raises, type hints on every signature, specific rather than bare exception handling, no hardcoded secrets, and an 80% coverage floor — the stated bar for the repo being 'production-grade' rather than sample code.

nodes.label: Example Project Scaffolding Convention
nodes.rationale: scripts/new-project.sh is mandated over hand-copying an existing project, so every projects/NN-name/ keeps the same isolated pyproject.toml + src/main.py + tests/ + README + .env.example shape and no drift accumulates between examples.

nodes.label: Flag-Gate New Framework Functionality
nodes.rationale: Contributors touching cockpit/ must check whether the module sits behind cockpit/config/feature_flags.py and keep experimental or tier-2/3 functionality flag-gated, so a deployment can exclude unfinished surface area without forking.

nodes.label: Per-Platform Deployment Checklist
nodes.rationale: Windows/Mac/Linux tracks share a Setup -> Secrets -> Testing -> Production phase order; Linux adds package-manager detection and NVIDIA CUDA / AMD ROCm GPU steps, Mac splits Ollama model choice by Intel (small models, CPU) vs Apple Silicon (larger models, GPU).

nodes.label: Multi-Machine Encrypted Secrets Distribution
nodes.rationale: Teams share .env.gpg through the repo and never .env; each member still runs secrets_cli init with their own keys, so a compromised clone exposes no plaintext credential.

nodes.label: Deployment Rollback Plan
nodes.rationale: Three tiers: local git reset --hard + uv sync --fresh, staged checkout of a stable branch + re-run setup, production git revert relying on CI/CD to redeploy — rollback is always a git operation, never a manual environment edit.

nodes.label: Deployment Success Criteria
nodes.rationale: Deployment is only 'done' when setup completes clean, the full suite passes, secrets load encrypted or from env, one project runs end-to-end, no keys appear in logs, provider rate limits and budgets are set, and rollback has been tested.

nodes.label: AI Engineering Cockpit Platform
nodes.rationale: Positioned as a production-grade AIDevOps platform: a modular cockpit/ framework plus 14 runnable example projects, with an explicit claim that every framework ships working logic rather than placeholders.

nodes.label: Layered Secrets Management
nodes.rationale: Four-tier first-match-wins resolution (env vars > encrypted .env.gpg > plaintext .env > external vault) lets the same code path serve development, team sharing, and production KMS without any project hardcoding a key or logging it in plaintext.

nodes.label: Six Core Frameworks
nodes.rationale: Testing, evaluation, red teaming, security, monitoring/governance, and configuration are each independently toggleable so a deployment only pays for the concerns it has.

nodes.label: Fourteen Example Projects
nodes.rationale: 01-05 are standalone and 06-14 import cockpit/ frameworks; every project is its own uv-managed package with mocked tests so pytest runs with no API key, and 06-14 expose --dry-run to demo before credentials exist.

nodes.label: Obfuscation-Aware Prompt Injection Detection
nodes.rationale: Scans raw input, a Unicode-normalized form (zero-width chars, letter-spacing, accented homoglyphs), and base64/hex/rot13 decodings, on the principle that an encoded instruction is still an instruction. Known coverage gap is stated honestly: 24 of 32 corpus payloads caught.

nodes.label: Self-Grading Red Team Harness
nodes.rationale: Runs a 32-payload injection corpus through the repo's own detector and reports which attacks slip past, so security blind spots are measured rather than assumed.

nodes.label: PII Masking with Luhn Validation
nodes.rationale: Credit-card masking runs a Luhn checksum before flagging, specifically to cut false positives that naive regex-only PII scanners produce on arbitrary 16-digit strings.

nodes.label: Tamper-Evident Audit Chain
nodes.rationale: The hash-chained audit log is documented as tamper-evident, not tamper-proof — it reveals modification but cannot prevent it; likewise compliance output yields evidence-based findings and never a pass/fail verdict, since compliance is a legal determination.

nodes.label: Cross-Platform Cloud vs Hybrid Support
nodes.rationale: All platforms run identical code; platform difference is opt-in configuration — Windows is cloud-only, Mac Intel gets CPU Ollama, Apple Silicon and Linux NVIDIA/AMD get GPU-accelerated Ollama.

nodes.label: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
nodes.rationale: GitHub Security Advisories is preferred over email because it keeps report, fix, and disclosure timeline in one private place; email exists for reporters without a GitHub account. Committed SLAs: 3 business days to acknowledge, 7 to assess, 90 to fix and disclose. Only `main` is supported since the project is pre-1.0.

nodes.label: Committed Secret Handling Policy
nodes.rationale: A hardcoded credential anywhere in the repo or its git history is classified as a vulnerability, not a bug, and must not be referenced in a public issue until rotated — disclosing the commit would point attackers at a live key.

nodes.label: Security Scope Boundary
nodes.rationale: In scope: cockpit/, projects/, .github/workflows/, scripts/. Out of scope: third-party dependency CVEs (primary fix belongs upstream), issues presupposing an already-compromised machine or .env, and social engineering — keeping triage focused on defects this repo can actually fix.

nodes.label: Platform Support Matrix
nodes.rationale: Windows, Mac Intel/Apple Silicon, and four Linux families are all 'fully supported'; only Ollama availability varies. No local Python install is required because uv manages the toolchain, removing the single most common onboarding failure.

nodes.label: Idempotent Setup Scripts
nodes.rationale: Every step checks current state before acting so the script is safe to re-run; the final step runs the root test suite with no API keys, guaranteeing a fresh clone passes immediately and any failure is environmental rather than credential-related.

nodes.label: Tool Config Lives in config/
nodes.rationale: pytest.ini, ruff.toml, and mypy.ini sit under config/ instead of the repo root to reduce root clutter; because none of those tools auto-discover configs there, every invocation outside the wrapper scripts must pass explicit flags (-c config/pytest.ini --rootdir=., --config config/ruff.toml, --config-file config/mypy.ini).

nodes.label: cockpit/ vs projects/ Split
nodes.rationale: The two halves intentionally do not share code at import time: cockpit/ carries cross-cutting concerns, projects/ stay readable top-to-bottom by a newcomer who knows nothing else about the repo.

nodes.label: Per-Project Dependency Isolation
nodes.rationale: Each project owns its pyproject.toml, .venv and lock, so one example's dependency change can never break another and each project README can stand alone as a self-sufficient tutorial.

nodes.label: Layered Design (Consumers, Cockpit, Providers)
nodes.rationale: Mermaid layering shows projects consuming config and utils directly while the six optional frameworks are reached only through is_enabled() gates, and providers (Gemini/OpenAI/Anthropic, plus Mac-only Ollama) sit outside the framework boundary.

nodes.label: Feature-Flag-Driven Modularity
nodes.rationale: FRAMEWORKS_ENABLED defaults all six to True — the flags exist so a deployment can drop what it does not need (research setups drop governance, cost-sensitive ones drop red-teaming), explicitly NOT because anything is unfinished. Code touching an optional framework calls is_enabled() and no-ops rather than erroring when disabled.

nodes.label: Use-Case Flag Profiles
nodes.rationale: get_use_case_flags() returns startup/enterprise/research/safety_focused presets shaped identically to FRAMEWORKS_ENABLED, so an operator picks a profile instead of hand-tuning six independent booleans.

nodes.label: Typical Request Data Flow
nodes.rationale: input -> project main -> config -> security -> provider client -> evaluation -> monitoring -> response, with every optional stage insertable independently; the pipeline still runs end to end with all optional frameworks off.

nodes.label: Gate Only at Entry Points
nodes.rationale: Pure computation (cost math, percentiles, hash-chain verification, permission lookups) is never flag-gated, on the reasoning that a flag should not take away the tools you need while investigating an incident.

nodes.label: Windows Cloud-Only vs Mac Hybrid Model Serving
nodes.rationale: Windows assumes no local model runtime; Mac adds an optional Ollama server at OLLAMA_HOST (default http://localhost:11434) for offline or cost-free experimentation, demonstrated by 05-hybrid-orchestrator's local/cloud routing.
nodes.norm_label: windows cloud-only vs mac hybrid model serving

nodes.label: Three-Tier Testing Surface
nodes.rationale: Root tests/ deliberately exercises only cockpit/config/* plus structural smoke checks and never reaches into framework internals, so it stays stable as frameworks evolve; deep tests are colocated with each framework and each project tests itself inside its own venv.

nodes.label: Gemini vs OpenAI vs Claude Comparison
nodes.rationale: Deliberately qualitative: exact prices and context windows change faster than a doc can track, so it describes pricing shape (per-token, output dearer than input, tiered by model class) and tells readers to verify live rate cards rather than trusting pasted numbers.

nodes.label: Provider Selection Guidance
nodes.rationale: Gemini for cost-sensitive or multimodal prototypes, OpenAI for the widest tooling ecosystem, Claude for long-context reasoning and strict instruction-following — but these are stated as tendencies, not benchmarks, with the recommended tiebreak being empirical comparison through 03-multi-model-orchestrator and cockpit/evaluation.

nodes.label: Track Observed Cost, Not Rate Cards
nodes.rationale: Cost tracking under the monitoring flag is named the right place to record actual per-call cost, because published rate cards drift and per-workload caching/batching changes effective spend.

nodes.label: ORION (Multi-Tool Orchestration Agent)
nodes.rationale: Project 15 of the cockpit. Takes one flagged transaction alert and produces escalate/clear/refer-to-human plus reasoning and an audit trail. KYC/AML was chosen as the domain because conflicting evidence is normal, every action must be auditable, and data-handling limits are real rather than decorative — which gives each mechanism something genuine to do. Explicitly distinct from 03-multi-model-orchestrator and 05-hybrid-orchestrator: ORION orchestrates tools, not models.

nodes.label: Dynamic Tool Registry
nodes.rationale: Tools are entries in a list that can change while the system runs, not hardcoded function calls. Registry holds a ToolSpec per tool (name, description, input schema, callable, permission scope, credibility score) and renders the tool list handed to the Tool Runner. Supports add/remove mid-run so the model's available capability surface is data rather than code.

nodes.label: Credibility Scoring
nodes.rationale: Exponential moving average score = (1-alpha)*score + alpha*outcome, outcome 1.0 success / 0.0 failure, alpha 0.2, initial 1.0, floor 0.1. A moving average rather than a success counter so recent behavior weighs more than distant history while a single failure does not destroy standing. The floor prevents a tool reaching zero and becoming permanently unusable — recoverable distrust, not a death sentence. Scores persist to JSON between runs so a tool that failed in one run starts the next trusted less, making credibility routing observable rather than asserted.

nodes.label: Permission Scoping (Scope Gate)
nodes.rationale: Before-hook enforcing field-level scope: each tool declares which alert fields it may receive, and a call carrying anything else is refused before the tool function executes, with the refusal returned to the model as an error result so it can retry differently. An operation dimension (read vs. write) was deliberately cut: all four v1 tools are read-only, so the check would have no case that could fail, and an unexercised permission check is worse than none — it looks like protection without being any. It belongs in the phase that first introduces a writing tool.

nodes.label: Conflict Resolution
nodes.rationale: Tool results normalize into claims (dimension, verdict, credibility of the producing tool); opposing verdicts on the same dimension are conflicts. A credibility gap above threshold 0.15 lets the more credible claim win, with the loser retained and marked overridden and the score gap recorded as justification; a gap at or below threshold produces no winner and resolves to 'needs human'. Declining to decide is a first-class outcome because in AML triage a near-arbitrary automated decision is worse than acknowledged uncertainty, and a resolver that always produces a winner would hide ambiguity rather than report it.

nodes.label: Anthropic Tool Runner Surface
nodes.rationale: The loop is driven by client.beta.messages.tool_runner from the anthropic Python SDK; the model chooses tools and order, the SDK runs request/execute/loop, and ORION's four mechanisms live in the per-turn before/after hooks. Chosen over two alternatives: the Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library and ships file/bash tools ORION has no use for, and is a separate product from the API SDK the rest of the cockpit uses; Managed Agents moves loop and sandbox onto Anthropic infrastructure, which is production-shaped but hides the orchestration this project exists to teach; a hand-written loop teaches most but discards a maintained implementation for no gain. Model: claude-opus-5, adaptive thinking.

nodes.label: Decision Rule (Verdict by Code)
nodes.rationale: A pure function from resolved claims to verdict, evaluated in order: unresolved conflict → needs human; surviving elevated-risk claim → escalate; otherwise clear. An overridden claim is not a surviving claim. The verdict is produced by code, not the model — the model writes only the narrative — because a regulated decision must be reproducible and explainable on demand, and a decision whose only provenance is a model's turn does not satisfy that. Same inputs and scores must always produce the same verdict.

nodes.label: ORION Audit Trail
nodes.rationale: Records every tool call: name, arguments as submitted, the scope gate's verdict, execution time, result or error, and credibility before and after — written alongside the decision as JSON so the whole run is reconstructable.

nodes.label: sanctions_screen (Simulated Tool)
nodes.rationale: Reliable watchlist screen reporting no match for the fixture customer. Makes the claim opposing transaction_graph on the customer-risk dimension — one half of the conflict the resolver exists to settle.

nodes.label: adverse_media_search (Simulated Tool)
nodes.rationale: Scripted to fail on first call with a timeout and succeed on retry, so the credibility drop and partial recovery are always exercised deterministically. Scoped to public-source data and explicitly may not receive the customer's national ID — sending an identity number to an external news service is the genuine privacy failure the scope gate exists to prevent.

nodes.label: transaction_graph (Simulated Tool)
nodes.rationale: Reports counterparties and their flags, including a link to a flagged entity. Its elevated-risk claim contradicts sanctions_screen's clear result on the same dimension, manufacturing the conflict the resolver must settle.

nodes.label: risk_score (Simulated Tool)
nodes.source_location: The simulated tools; How a case flows
nodes.rationale: 0-100 composite requiring the other three results as input. The dependency is real rather than declared: the model calls it only once the first wave lands, so sequencing emerges from the model's planning rather than a scheduler.

nodes.label: Emergent Parallelism and Sequencing
nodes.rationale: The model has no reason to sequence sanctions, media and graph, so it requests all three in one turn and they execute concurrently; risk_score depends on their results so it is called in a second wave. Parallelism and ordering come from the model's planning rather than from a scheduler, which is the point of a model-driven loop.

nodes.label: Offline Deterministic Test Strategy
nodes.rationale: Every test but one runs offline with no API key; simulated tools' failures are scripted so the suite is deterministic. The loop is tested with a mocked SDK client returning a canned tool-call sequence, asserting hook ordering with no tokens spent. One live end-to-end test is marked and skipped by default — it is the only proof the wiring works, so it exists, but it never blocks the suite.

nodes.label: ORION v1 Deferred Capabilities
nodes.rationale: Fallback to a different tool on failure needs two tools covering one capability; with four distinct tools there is nothing to fall back to, so only retry is implemented. Mid-run escalation to the user is covered by the needs-human verdict. Real external APIs would break offline determinism. A dashboard and batch processing are already covered by 08-cost-dashboard and 10-batch-pipeline.

nodes.label: Learning-First Design Constraint
nodes.rationale: The author is building ORION to learn the mechanics, not only to demonstrate them. That constraint shapes the architecture: mechanisms stay small, separately testable units rather than being folded into a framework, and the build proceeds test-first with the author writing the implementation code.

nodes.label: ORION Phases 0-1 Implementation Plan
nodes.rationale: Stands up the project skeleton then builds the dynamic tool registry and four simulated tools. Explicitly not for autonomous execution: the author writes the implementation by hand as a learning exercise and Claude supplies tests and review.

nodes.label: Tests-Shown, Bodies-Withheld Plan Format
nodes.source_location: How this plan differs from the standard format
nodes.rationale: The writing-plans format requires every step to show code; this plan shows every test in full but deliberately omits implementation bodies, giving only signature, docstring contract and required behaviour. That is not a placeholder — handing over the bodies would defeat the author's stated goal of writing the implementation and being coached. Anyone executing the plan who is not the author is told to stop and ask first.

nodes.label: ToolSpec (Frozen Dataclass)
nodes.rationale: Fields: name, description, input_schema, run callable, allowed_fields frozenset of dotted alert paths. Frozen because a spec is configuration, not state — a spec that mutates mid-run is one that can be mutated by accident. allowed_fields is a frozenset rather than a set because a frozen dataclass containing a mutable set is only shallowly frozen and the set could still be mutated in place.

nodes.label: Registry Class (add/remove/get/names)
nodes.rationale: Construction routes through add so the duplicate-name check is written once and applies to construction too; duplicate names are refused because two tools with one name make the model's call ambiguous. The default arg is an empty tuple rather than a list to avoid the shared-mutable-default trap. to_tool_params renders only name, description and input_schema — allowed_fields is ORION's own business for the scope gate and would be a meaningless key in the API request.

nodes.label: Sorted Tool List for Prompt-Cache Stability
nodes.rationale: Registry.names() sorts rather than preserving insertion order because prompt caching keys on an exact prefix and the tool list is part of that prefix. A registry returning insertion order would silently invalidate the cached prefix whenever registration order changed. to_tool_params reuses names() rather than re-sorting so the ordering rule lives in one place.
nodes.norm_label: sorted tool list for prompt-cache stability

nodes.label: make_adverse_media_search Factory
nodes.rationale: A factory returning a closure that keeps its own call count, raising ToolTimeoutError on the first fail_times calls. State lives in the closure because a module-level counter would leak between tests and runs — the second caller would get a pass where a failure was expected, silently retiring the retry path. fail_times is configurable so Phase 3 can drive a credibility score to the floor.

nodes.label: build_registry()
nodes.rationale: Constructs one ToolSpec per tool and returns the populated Registry that Phases 2, 3 and 4 all start from. It is a function rather than a module-level constant because it calls make_adverse_media_search() and a module-level registry would share one failure counter across every run in the process. input_schema is hand-written per tool rather than generated from signatures because the schema is what the model reads to build its call.

nodes.label: EXPECTED_SCOPES Permission Declarations
nodes.rationale: The declared allowed_fields per tool, called the single most important assertion in Phase 1: Phase 2's gate is only as good as this declaration, so if customer.national_id ever appears in adverse_media_search's scope the gate will dutifully permit the leak it exists to prevent. risk_score declares an empty frozenset because it consumes other tools' findings, never customer data.

nodes.label: alert-001.json Fixture
nodes.rationale: A single flagged transaction (STRUCTURING_PATTERN, customer CUST-88421 Marek Dvorak CZ, counterparty Vantage Freight OU EE). The scaffold test asserts national_id is present specifically so that removing it — which would silently turn the Phase 2 scope-gate tests into no-ops — fails loudly instead.

nodes.label: Deviation: src/tools.py Instead of tools/ Package
nodes.rationale: The spec says tools/. Four functions of about thirty lines each that change together come to one readable module; a package of four single-function modules plus __init__.py is four times the files for no gain in isolation. Revisit when a tool grows a real HTTP client.
nodes.norm_label: deviation: src/tools.py instead of tools/ package

nodes.label: Deviation: Credibility Scores Not Stored on ToolSpec
nodes.rationale: The spec says the registry entry holds the tool's current score; the plan freezes ToolSpec as pure configuration and leaves scores to the Phase 3 store keyed by tool name — which is how they are persisted to JSON anyway. Score is state with a completely different lifecycle from tool identity. test_tool_spec_is_immutable encodes the decision so reversing it means deleting a test on purpose rather than drifting.
nodes.norm_label: deviation: credibility scores not stored on toolspec

nodes.label: Extract-Don't-Deploy Deployment Stance
nodes.rationale: The repo is an MVP/learning platform, not a production deployment framework. Projects are meant to be read, understood and extracted into a production codebase rather than deployed as-is from the monorepo. Deploy one self-contained project directory, re-pin with uv lock and build from uv sync --frozen so production installs exactly what was tested.

nodes.label: Platform-Injected Secrets
nodes.rationale: Never ship .env or commit real keys; set provider keys as real environment variables injected by the platform's secret store (container env store, serverless secrets manager injected at cold-start not build time, or a systemd EnvironmentFile with restricted permissions). cockpit/config/settings.py reads keys via os.getenv through get_settings(), so moving from local .env to a real secrets manager needs no code change as long as the variables exist at process start.

nodes.label: Implemented Is Not Sufficient (Honest Gap Disclosure)
nodes.source_location: What this repo does not give you
nodes.rationale: Every framework is implemented, but implemented is not the same as sufficient for your obligations. Two limits are documented rather than hidden: the injection filter catches 24 of 32 corpus payloads and is structurally blind to cross-turn attacks, and compliance.py reports findings and evidence while deliberately emitting no compliance verdict because that is a legal determination software does not get to make. The audit log is tamper-evident (a hash chain revealing modification), not tamper-proof — a real control anchors the head hash where the application cannot rewrite it.
nodes.norm_label: implemented is not sufficient (honest gap disclosure)

nodes.label: Idempotent Setup Scripts
nodes.rationale: setup-windows.ps1 and setup-mac.sh install uv, pin Python 3.11+, run uv sync --all-groups, copy .env.example to .env and run the suite as a sanity check. Both are idempotent so they can be re-run at any time without side effects — a fresh clone to a first working example in five minutes.

nodes.label: Documentation Index
nodes.rationale: The map newcomers use to find their way around the repo, split into start-here, reference and recipes. Explicit policy: if a doc goes stale, prefer fixing it over deleting it.

nodes.label: Prompt-Injection Filter Coverage
nodes.rationale: scan_for_prompt_injection flags 24 of 32 red-team corpus payloads (75%), up from 12 of 32 (37.5%) in the first version — measured from a real run, not estimated, and reproducible via 07-red-team-runner --gap-only. The honest framing: a request-time regex filter is a cheap first layer whose job is to make easy attacks expensive, not a security boundary, and 75% is not a passing grade for anything you would call a control.

nodes.label: Three-Surface Scanning (Raw / Normalized / Decoded)
nodes.rationale: Matching literal text is trivially defeated, so the same pattern set runs over three surfaces: raw input; normalized (NFKD, combining marks stripped, invisible characters removed, letter-spacing collapsed, then recomposed) to defeat obfuscation that destroys surface form while preserving meaning for the tokenizer; and decoded (base64, hex, rot13) because an encoded instruction is still an instruction the model will decode. A hit on any surface other than raw is reported as such, because input that only looks like an attack after de-obfuscation is more suspicious, not less.

nodes.label: NFKD-Before-NFKC Normalization Order
nodes.rationale: NFKC composes i + U+0301 into an accented character, so stripping combining marks afterwards does nothing and accented homoglyphs sail through; the fix is NFKD first, strip marks, then NFKC. Letter-spacing must also be collapsed per span rather than per word, because a per-word rule needs a minimum run length and short words fall under it, which breaks the phrase match for the whole sentence.

nodes.label: Payload Splitting as a Structural Blind Spot
nodes.rationale: 0/3 caught, and a structural limit rather than an oversight: the malicious instruction never appears intact in any single message, being assembled from fragments, deferred references or reversal that the model itself resolves. A stateless per-message filter has nothing to match; catching it needs conversation-level state, and pretending a regex will handle it would be worse than documenting it. The remaining misses carry no injection-specific vocabulary, and chasing each would overfit to 32 known payloads — the corpus is a sample of techniques, not the population of attacks.
nodes.norm_label: payload splitting as a structural blind spot

nodes.label: Filter Coverage vs. Model Resistance
nodes.rationale: Two independent measurements reported separately: does the request-time scan see the attack, and does the target actually comply when attacked. They are not substitutes — delimiter_escape was fully caught by the filter even in the original version yet all four payloads still succeed against a naive target, and a payload the filter misses may still be refused by a well-prompted model.

nodes.label: Windows Cloud-Only / Mac Hybrid Platform Split
nodes.rationale: Ollama's local-model runtime and the surrounding tooling ecosystem is most mature on macOS and Linux. Rather than pretend Windows support is equivalent and let people hit broken, half-tested local-model code, the line is drawn explicitly: Windows is cloud-only with OLLAMA_HOST present for consistency but unused; Mac is hybrid. This keeps Windows setup free of GPU-driver and local-runtime debugging while letting Mac users exploit local inference for cost-free experimentation, offline development and privacy-sensitive testing.
nodes.norm_label: windows cloud-only / mac hybrid platform split

nodes.label: No Runtime OS Branch in Shared Framework
nodes.rationale: No code in cockpit/ hard-codes an OS check; the split is enforced by which examples you choose to run rather than by a runtime branch, which keeps the shared framework code identical across platforms. New hybrid examples should keep local and cloud paths in separate modules behind a small router so Windows users can simply never import the local module.
nodes.norm_label: no runtime os branch in shared framework

nodes.label: Minimal RAG Loop Recipe
nodes.rationale: retrieve -> build_prompt -> generate. Retrieval is deliberately separate from generation so the implementation can move from keyword match to embeddings to a vector database without touching prompt construction or the model call. The prompt explicitly tells the model to stick to the context and admit when it cannot answer — described as the single highest-leverage change for reducing hallucination in a RAG system. An empty document set raises RuntimeError rather than silently asking the model to answer from nothing.

nodes.label: Embeddings Are Not Comparable Across Models
nodes.rationale: Vectors from different embedding models occupy different spaces, so switching embedding models requires re-embedding the entire corpus rather than mixing old and new vectors. gemini-embedding-001 produces 3072-dimensional vectors.
nodes.norm_label: embeddings are not comparable across models

nodes.label: ChatSession with Bounded History
nodes.rationale: MAX_HISTORY_TURNS caps context growth so neither the window nor the bill grows without limit over a long conversation, tuned per provider context window and latency/cost budget. to_messages() returns the provider-agnostic {role, content} shape all three supported providers accept, so the session object is not tied to one SDK. Role validation raises early rather than silently corrupting the conversation. For very long conversations, summarize dropped turns rather than discarding them.

nodes.label: Provider-Agnostic Streaming Pattern
nodes.rationale: Iterator[str] keeps the contract provider-agnostic — the caller depends only on an iterator of string chunks, so swapping SDKs does not change consuming code. Callers accumulate as they go rather than re-requesting a non-streamed call. With google-genai a chunk's .text is None when the chunk carries no text part, so falsy chunks are skipped at the provider boundary to keep the Iterator[str] contract honest. Consumption is wrapped in try/except with logger.exception so a dropped connection surfaces as a clear error rather than a truncated response that looks complete.

nodes.label: Ollama Hybrid-Mode Assets
nodes.rationale: A Modelfile builds cockpit-assistant on top of llama3 with a project-specific system prompt; it is tested from the CLI first so a Python failure can be attributed to the client rather than the model. Python calls go to settings.ollama_host/api/generate, defaulting to http://localhost:11434 and read from OLLAMA_HOST.

nodes.label: 01-hello-world (Gemini Sanity Check)
nodes.rationale: The simplest possible working Gemini call — read a key from the environment, send one prompt, print the response — existing as the 'does my key work and is the SDK wired up correctly' check before anything more complex. Fully standalone with its own pyproject.toml, importing nothing from the rest of the repo. Tests mock the SDK so no key or network is needed.

nodes.label: google-genai SDK Migration
nodes.rationale: Uses the current google-genai SDK with genai.Client(api_key=...) and gemini-2.5-flash, because the older google-generativeai package is end-of-life and the gemini-1.5-* model ids it was usually paired with now return HTTP 404.

nodes.label: Ruflo Coordination Ledger and Implementation Loop
nodes.rationale: Ruflo is the coordination ledger and policy decision point while Claude Code is the executor. Registered, configured, reachable, healthy and authorized are treated as separate facts rather than one boolean. Claims and evidence bind to exact source/build receipts, and publication only happens through a separately authorized release gate. Note: the ORION spec records that ruflo is not installed as a plugin and nothing in that design depends on it — these artifacts are untracked leftovers from a prior claude-flow initialization.
nodes.norm_label: ruflo coordination ledger and implementation loop

nodes.label: Capability Attenuation and Single-Writer Ownership
nodes.rationale: Never two writers in one worktree: each writing agent gets an isolated worktree and explicit file ownership, and only the integration owner edits shared manifests and lockfiles. A child may drop capabilities but cannot add tools, network, secrets, spend, concurrency, namespaces or delegation depth. A lease or claim coordinates ownership; it does not authorize a side effect. Subsystems may propose or evaluate candidates but cannot self-promote or expand their safety envelope.

nodes.label: SendMessage-First Agent Coordination
nodes.rationale: Named agents coordinate by direct messaging rather than polling or shared state. All agents spawn in one message with run_in_background, each prompt naming who to message next; the lead then continues independent local work and waits only when a dependency genuinely blocks. Patterns: pipeline for sequential dependencies, fan-out for independent parallel work, supervisor for ongoing coordination.

nodes.label: 3-Tier Model Routing and Swarm Thresholds
nodes.rationale: Route to the smallest capable topology: tier 1 WASM transforms skip the LLM entirely and use Edit directly, tier 2 Haiku handles low-complexity tasks, tier 3 Sonnet/Opus takes architecture, security and complex reasoning. Swarming is reserved for 3+ files, new features, cross-module refactors, API changes, security and performance — never single-file edits, 1-2 line fixes, docs or questions.

nodes.label: 02-rag-chatbot
nodes.rationale: Chunk, embed, retrieve, augment, generate — a runnable RAG demo. Standalone with its own pyproject.toml, with every SDK boundary mocked or injected in tests so the suite needs no key or network.

nodes.label: Real Embeddings Over Local TF-IDF
nodes.rationale: Calls the real gemini-embedding-001 endpoint rather than hand-rolling a local embedding such as TF-IDF with difflib, because that keeps retrieval quality realistic — it captures meaning rather than word overlap. The cost is network access and an API key at runtime; embeddings.py isolates every SDK call behind small functions so the code stays unit-testable offline.

nodes.label: Brute-Force Retrieval Without a Vector Database
nodes.rationale: Every chunk embedding is compared against the query with cosine similarity and sorted — a linear scan, with no vector database on purpose: for a handful of documents plain Python is fast and far simpler than standing up Chroma/Pinecone/Weaviate. Chunking is by blank-line paragraphs, the simplest strategy keeping each chunk topically coherent for a small corpus, and explicitly not appropriate for long or unstructured documents, which need fixed-size or sentence-aware chunking with overlap.
nodes.norm_label: brute-force retrieval without a vector database

nodes.label: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
nodes.rationale: Combines a retrieval step with generation so the model can answer over documents it never saw in training, and so answers are grounded in a source rather than invented.

nodes.label: Text Embeddings
nodes.rationale: Texts with similar meaning produce vectors pointing in similar directions; that property is what retrieval systems rely on.

nodes.label: Vector Database
nodes.rationale: Deliberately NOT used in this demo: for a few documents a full vector DB is unnecessary overhead, and brute-force cosine comparison in plain Python is fast enough and far simpler to reason about.

nodes.label: Cosine Similarity
nodes.rationale: Measures angle rather than magnitude, so it is insensitive to document length — which is why it is the popular metric for text embeddings.

nodes.label: Document Chunking
nodes.rationale: Trade-off: smaller chunks retrieve more precisely because each covers a narrower topic, but too-small chunks lose surrounding context. Paragraph boundaries are the chosen starting point.

nodes.label: Prompt Augmentation
nodes.rationale: Injecting retrieved chunks with an 'answer using only the context below' instruction keeps the answer grounded in retrieved text and makes citation possible.

nodes.label: Uniform generate(prompt) -> str Interface
nodes.rationale: Both vendor wrappers expose the identical interface, which is what makes them interchangeable to the orchestrator and lets cost-based routing, A/B testing, or ensemble voting be layered on later without touching client code.

nodes.label: Side-by-Side Provider Comparison
nodes.rationale: No single model is uniformly best — latency, tone, factuality and cost vary by provider and task, so measure latency, quality trade-offs and failover resilience before committing a product to one vendor.

nodes.label: Per-Provider Error Isolation
nodes.rationale: Latency and success/failure are recorded independently per provider so one provider failing does not stop the others; a missing API key skips that provider with a warning rather than crashing the run.

nodes.label: google-genai SDK Migration (legacy package EOL)
nodes.rationale: One genai.Client built at construction, model id passed per request. The legacy google-generativeai package (genai.configure + GenerativeModel) is end-of-life; gemini-1.5-* ids are retired and return HTTP 404, so gemini-2.5-flash is the default.

nodes.label: Streaming vs Non-Streaming Generation
nodes.rationale: Streaming buys perceived latency (output appears in hundreds of ms instead of feeling frozen), early cancellation (stop paying for tokens you will discard), and progressive rendering. Cost: consuming an iterator is more complex and you cannot easily retry or post-process until fully assembled.

nodes.label: iter_chunks (None-text chunk filter)
nodes.rationale: A chunk's .text can legitimately be None because the SDK emits metadata-only chunks, so the empty-chunk filter is load-bearing: without it, assembling the response fails on a None.

nodes.label: Composable Decomposition for Offline Testability
nodes.rationale: Splitting the module into small pieces is what lets tests hand start_stream a mock client returning a plain Python iterator of mock chunks (including a text=None chunk) and assert on assembled output, with no real network stream.

nodes.label: google-genai Streaming SDK Usage
nodes.rationale: Uses client.models.generate_content_stream; the legacy google-generativeai per-model GenerativeModel(generate_content(..., stream=True)) path is end-of-life and gemini-1.5-* ids return HTTP 404.

nodes.label: Project 05 - Hybrid Orchestrator (Local Ollama + Cloud Gemini)
nodes.norm_label: project 05 - hybrid orchestrator (local ollama + cloud gemini)

nodes.label: HybridRouter
nodes.rationale: The same router runs unmodified on Mac and Windows; behaviour differs only because of what is actually reachable at OLLAMA_HOST, so there is no separate 'Windows mode' code path.

nodes.label: LocalOllamaClient
nodes.rationale: is_available() does a short-timeout GET /api/tags; any failure (connection refused, DNS failure, timeout) is treated as 'local not available' rather than an error to propagate.

nodes.label: Prompt-Length Complexity Heuristic
nodes.rationale: Prompts at or under HYBRID_LOCAL_MAX_PROMPT_CHARS (default 400) route local on the assumption a small local model handles short prompts fine; longer prompts go to cloud.

nodes.label: Graceful, Non-Exceptional Fallback
nodes.rationale: An unreachable Ollama never crashes the program: every connection failure becomes False or a caught OllamaUnavailableError, and the router treats both as 'use cloud'. HybridRouter.generate() only raises when the cloud backend also fails — the one point where there is nowhere left to fall back to.

nodes.label: HybridResult (backend_used, fallback_occurred, reason)
nodes.rationale: Records which backend actually answered, whether a fallback occurred, and why — so logs show which path a given request took instead of leaving it a guess.

nodes.label: google-genai SDK in Cloud Backend
nodes.rationale: Same migration stance as projects 03 and 04: one genai.Client at construction, model id per request, legacy google-generativeai is EOL, gemini-1.5-* returns 404.

nodes.label: Injected generate_fn (harness imports no LLM SDK)
nodes.rationale: Taking an injected generate_fn(prompt) -> str is why the whole suite runs with no API key and no network, and why the harness can be pointed at a raw model client, a RAG pipeline, or an agent loop without changing a line of harness code.
nodes.norm_label: injected generate_fn (harness imports no llm sdk)

nodes.label: UsageReporter vs 4-chars-per-token Estimate
nodes.rationale: With a UsageReporter the harness prices live runs from the provider's real usage_metadata; without one it falls back to a documented ~4-chars-per-token estimate and prints '(token counts estimated from text length)' rather than quietly pretending the number is exact.

nodes.label: 12-item Reference Eval Set
nodes.rationale: Every reference answer is short, factual and checkable without external context, so token-overlap and keyword metrics actually mean something.

nodes.label: Loud Dataset Validation (DatasetError)
nodes.rationale: Missing fields, duplicate item_ids, a bare string where a keyword list belongs, and unparseable JSON all raise with the offending location named, rather than producing a silently wrong scorecard three layers up.

nodes.label: 0.35 Pass Threshold Calibration
nodes.rationale: The metrics are lexical, so a correct answer phrased differently lands around 0.55-0.75, not 0.95. Setting the bar where correct paraphrases actually land is the difference between a useful gate and one everybody disables.

nodes.label: Deliberately Imperfect Canned Answer Bank
nodes.rationale: A harness that always reports 100% is a harness that is not measuring anything, so q-009 gets a vague non-answer and q-011 a confidently wrong expansion of ACID — proving the scoring discriminates.

nodes.label: package = false + pythonpath Bridge to cockpit/
nodes.rationale: The repo root is deliberately not installed into the subproject venv; pythonpath = ["src", "../.."] plus a small sys.path insert put it on the import path instead.
nodes.norm_label: package = false + pythonpath bridge to cockpit/

nodes.label: Defense-Coverage Gap Report
nodes.rationale: Most red-team output tells you how one model behaved on one day and expires when you swap models. The gap report asks the durable question instead — how many known techniques the request-time filter flags at all. Answer: 12 of 32; 20 payloads reach the model untouched. Deliberately does not flip the exit code, because it is a finding about the filter, not the target.

nodes.label: cockpit.security.input_security (scan_for_prompt_injection)
nodes.rationale: Its own docstring calls it a heuristic regex pre-filter that will not catch novel or obfuscated injection; this project turns that caveat into a number you can put in a review. Regex pre-filtering is a speed bump, not a control.

nodes.label: Fully Blind Attack Categories
nodes.rationale: encoding_obfuscation (base64/ROT13/letter-spacing/zero-width), payload_splitting, and refusal_suppression are 0% detected: the surface string changed or there is no injection phrasing at all. system_prompt_leak sits at 20% while carrying two critical evading payloads.

nodes.label: build_canary_probe (system-prompt canary)
nodes.rationale: Planting a fresh high-entropy token turns 'did the system prompt leak?' from a judgement call into an exact string test; without a canary, leak payloads can only ever score as defended, so the report records that the pass rate is optimistic.

nodes.label: Refusing / Naive / Brittle Control Targets
nodes.rationale: A harness that always reports 'all clear' is indistinguishable from one that is broken, so two offline stubs pin the ends of the scale and a test asserts the gap between them exceeds 0.4. Filter coverage and model resistance are independent measurements: delimiter_escape is 4/4 caught by the filter yet 4/4 landed against NaiveTarget.

nodes.label: InstrumentedClient (instrument the call once)
nodes.rationale: The usual failure mode is bolting cost and latency on in two unrelated places and then finding they disagree about how many calls happened; wrapping the model call exactly once removes that class of bug. A failing call is still booked as an error latency sample instead of vanishing from the distribution.

nodes.label: extract_usage (defensive token extraction)
nodes.rationale: Cost comes from real usage_metadata counts, not a character-count guess; a response with no usage metadata yields zeros rather than raising, so an unusual response shape degrades the dashboard instead of killing the run.

nodes.label: Own Trackers Instead of Module Globals
nodes.rationale: The monitoring framework exposes process-wide default trackers, but globals would make tests order-dependent and prevent showing two runs side by side. Latency is also read off the measurement handle rather than the tracker's sample list so nothing races when calls are fanned out.
nodes.norm_label: own trackers instead of module globals

nodes.label: PRICING_VERIFIED_DATE (dated default price table)
nodes.rationale: The price table is a dated default printed after every run as a reminder ('override it before trusting it'), with a pricing= override for negotiated or newer rates.

nodes.label: Injectable Fake Clock for Reproducible Output
nodes.rationale: --dry-run fakes the clock as well as the model, so the offline demo records an exact 0.250s per call and produces reproducible output rather than reflecting how fast the machine happened to be. PerformanceTracker.measure reads the clock exactly twice per call.
nodes.norm_label: injectable fake clock for reproducible output

nodes.label: Project 09 - Agent Tool Use (LLM Function Calling)
nodes.norm_label: project 09 - agent tool use (llm function calling)

nodes.label: Manual Function Calling Mode
nodes.rationale: Disabling automatic calling hands you the proposed call instead of executing it. It is the only mode with a place for an authorization check, audit-log write, or human approval, and the only one giving a real trace — required when a tool has side effects. The trade-off is code: a loop, a maintained transcript, and an error path per failure mode.

nodes.label: ToolUseAgent (injected model client)
nodes.rationale: The model client is injected, never constructed inside the loop, which is what makes the whole thing testable offline. Automatic mode still produces a trace via functools.wraps recording wrappers that keep the SDK-derived schema unchanged.

nodes.label: Docstrings Are the Tool Spec
nodes.rationale: The SDK turns the summary line into the tool description and Args: entries into parameter descriptions — literally how the model learns what a tool does. A vague docstring is a vague tool, so tests assert every tool has one with full annotations.

nodes.label: calculate (AST allowlist arithmetic)
nodes.rationale: eval() on model text is arbitrary code execution, so the expression is parsed with ast.parse(mode='eval') and walked against a node-type allowlist — rejection is by node type, not by blocklisting scary substrings. bool is rejected explicitly since it subclasses int; exponentiation is bounded so 9**9**9 cannot hang the process.

nodes.label: ToolRegistry as Authorization Allowlist
nodes.rationale: registry.get(name) is the single place a model-proposed name is resolved, so an unregistered name has nowhere else to go: refused, never executed, recorded as authorized=False, and fed back as a function_response error so the model can recover.

nodes.label: Iteration Cap on the Agent Loop
nodes.rationale: A model that keeps asking for tools gets StopReason.ITERATION_CAP rather than unbounded spend; automatic mode gets the same bound via AutomaticFunctionCallingConfig(maximum_remote_calls=...).
nodes.norm_label: iteration cap on the agent loop

nodes.label: Input and Output Screening
nodes.rationale: validate_input gates the question before the model sees it; every tool result is screened with detect_pii_leakage BEFORE being appended to the transcript, because a tool result is untrusted data heading into the model's context and back out to the user; detect_refusal makes 'the model declined' a reported outcome rather than something to grep for.

nodes.label: Recoverable Tool Errors
nodes.rationale: A ToolError or wrong-argument call does not abort the run; the error text goes back to the model as {"error": ...}, giving it a chance to retry correctly.

nodes.label: Cockpit Instrumentation Module
nodes.rationale: Model calls and tool executions are timed under separate operation names (model.generate vs tool.calculate) so a slow tool is distinguishable from a slow model; refused calls are deliberately not timed because nothing ran. An unpriced model id contributes 0 rather than being fatal.

nodes.label: fake_client (SDK response-tree replica)
nodes.rationale: Reproduces the part of the SDK response tree the agent actually reads and emulates automatic function calling by invoking the callables in config.tools, which makes --dry-run a faithful demo rather than a stub. The requests the agent builds are genuine google.genai.types objects, so the suite also pins the SDK call shape.

nodes.label: Pure Local Tools (zero blast radius)
nodes.rationale: Four tools with no network, no filesystem writes, no subprocesses. That property is what makes automatic mode defensible at all: if the model can invoke a function with no human in the loop, the blast radius of a wrong call needs to be roughly zero.

nodes.label: run_batch (injected process_fn)
nodes.rationale: The unit of work is injected as process_fn(InputRecord) -> ProcessOutput, so nothing imports an SDK at module scope and the whole suite runs with no API key and no network.

nodes.label: Token-Bucket Rate Limiting
nodes.rationale: Each record acquires a token first so a 5,000-record file cannot machine-gun the provider into a 429 storm; a record that cannot get capacity within acquire_timeout_seconds is failed rather than blocking the run forever. The limiter is a Protocol, not a hard dependency, which is what makes throttling tests deterministic.

nodes.label: Selective Retry (TransientError only)
nodes.rationale: Only TransientError is retried — a ValueError from bad input is a bug, and retrying it just burns three times the money for the same wrong answer. The live Gemini process_fn deliberately re-raises everything as TransientError because distinguishing a retryable 429 from a permanent 400 needs provider-specific inspection, and that limit is documented rather than hidden.

nodes.label: Partial-Failure Tolerance
nodes.rationale: run_batch never raises on a per-record failure: the batch always finishes and always reports which records didn't, via BatchResult.errors.

nodes.label: Attempts Timed Individually, Records Billed Once
nodes.rationale: A record succeeding on its second try contributes two latency samples (one an error) and exactly one cost entry; timing the whole retry loop as one sample would hide the retry and blend backoff sleep into 'model latency'. Failed records cost nothing in the ledger but their attempts still appear in latency and error-rate data.
nodes.norm_label: attempts timed individually, records billed once

nodes.label: Separately Injected Elapsed-Time Clock
nodes.rationale: run_batch's elapsed clock is injected separately from the PerformanceTracker's clock so throughput assertions are exact; backoff is 1ms in tests; throttle counts use a FakeLimiter, while one test drives the real RateLimiter and asserts only a lower bound because token-bucket refill depends on monotonic-clock granularity and an exact count there would be flaky.

nodes.label: Five-Stage Refusable Gateway Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Authorize, validate input, invoke, sanitize output, audit — every request runs the same pipeline and each stage can refuse. The model call is injected as generate_fn so tests and --dry-run need no API key.

nodes.label: mask_pii (output_security stage)
nodes.rationale: Runs before the response is returned OR logged, so a log line cannot become the leak.

nodes.label: Refusals Are Audited Too
nodes.rationale: A gateway that only records what it allowed tells you nothing about what someone tried; the denied attempts are the interesting ones, and tests assert a refused request still produces an audit record and never reached the model.

nodes.label: Secret (self-redacting API key holder)
nodes.rationale: Redacts through every string-formatting path so a stray log line or traceback cannot leak a key.

nodes.label: LEGAL_TRANSITIONS map
nodes.rationale: development -> production is simply not in the map, so reaching production requires passing through staging — this stops shipping straight from a developer's branch to live traffic.

nodes.label: cockpit.governance.approval_workflow
nodes.rationale: Production requires an approved request; rejection is terminal — a rejected request cannot be walked back to approved by collecting more signatures afterwards.

nodes.label: No Self-Approval Control
nodes.rationale: The requester cannot approve their own request: an approval process a single person can complete alone is theatre. Approvals are also deduplicated by principal, not by call, so one approver cannot defeat a 2-of-M threshold by approving twice.

nodes.label: cockpit.governance.model_versioning (ModelRegistry)
nodes.rationale: Exactly one version in production: promoting a new version atomically demotes the incumbent, removing ambiguity about what is actually serving.

nodes.label: cockpit.governance.audit_trail (GovernanceTrail)
nodes.rationale: Registry and workflow write to the module-level default trail automatically; build your own GovernanceTrail when you need isolation.

nodes.label: Refusal-First Scripted Transcript
nodes.rationale: The scripted demo shows a straight-to-production attempt, an unapproved promotion and a self-approval, each blocked with the reason — a pipeline demo where nothing is ever refused demonstrates nothing. Injected timestamps make the transcript identical every run.

nodes.label: Findings and Evidence, Never a Verdict
nodes.rationale: Software can evidence that specific automated checks ran and what they found; compliance is a legal and organizational determination made by counsel or an auditor from context a program cannot see. A tool printing 'COMPLIANT: TRUE' would eventually be shown to an auditor, which is genuinely harmful — so there is no pass/fail, no score, no boolean, and a test asserting that. --fail-on encodes an operator's chosen threshold, not a compliance judgment.
nodes.norm_label: findings and evidence, never a verdict

nodes.label: Controls That Did Not Run
nodes.rationale: Every report reproduces the framework DISCLAIMER and lists controls that did not run, because a report generated from missing inputs must not be mistakable for a clean one: absence of findings is not evidence of compliance.

nodes.label: GDPR Controls
nodes.rationale: Subject access export, erasure with legal-hold and retention exceptions surfaced rather than silently skipped, portability, consent validity, retention windows.

nodes.label: HIPAA Controls
nodes.rationale: PHI found in fields not designated to hold it, plus a minimum-necessary check against a declared purpose.

nodes.label: SOX Controls (segregation of duties)
nodes.rationale: Detects the same principal requesting and approving a change, plus change-audit completeness.

nodes.label: Synthetic Adversarial Dataset
nodes.rationale: data/records.json is fabricated and deliberately contains a record past retention, one under legal hold, PHI in the wrong field and a self-approved change, so every control has something to find. Subject ids include subj-1 and subj-10 specifically so a substring-matching export bug — which would be a real data breach — gets caught.

nodes.label: cockpit.security.threat_detection
nodes.rationale: Reads either a saved JSONL event stream or a live AuditLog hash chain and turns it into ranked, investigable findings.

nodes.label: Behavioral Detector Suite
nodes.rationale: Brute force (repeated auth failures in a window), data exfiltration (reading far above an actor's norm), privilege escalation (actions beyond a role, or a role change followed immediately by sensitive access), and anomalous rate (volume above the actor's own baseline).

nodes.label: Every Finding Carries Its Evidence
nodes.rationale: An alert you cannot investigate is noise — you cannot action 'suspicious activity detected' without knowing which requests, when, and by whom. Long evidence is elided in the middle with a marker telling you how to see the rest.

nodes.label: Heuristics Need Tuning (false-positive direction)
nodes.rationale: Behavioral detection trades false positives against misses and the right balance depends on your traffic; the bundled defaults suit the sample stream, not production. The sample stream carries substantial benign traffic and one test asserts a benign-only stream produces zero findings, because a detector that fires on everything is as useless as one that fires on nothing.

nodes.label: Scoping Narrows the Whole Report
nodes.rationale: --actor narrows the actor roster too: a report claiming to be about one principal should not enumerate who else was in the stream.

nodes.label: Python Project CI Workflow
nodes.rationale: Runs lint (ruff), format check (black), type check (mypy), security scan (bandit -ll) and pytest with coverage across Python 3.11 and 3.12. The step order is deliberately identical to `make check`: if CI and local ever diverge, the one that is green stops meaning anything.

nodes.label: Pre-commit Hook Set
nodes.rationale: black's --line-length must match pyproject.toml, or black and ruff rewrite each other's work on every commit. Also includes detect-private-key and check-added-large-files as commit-time guards.

nodes.label: Injected Provider Clients Convention
nodes.rationale: Provider clients are injected, never constructed inside the logic — that is what lets tests run with no API key, no network, and no flakiness. --dry-run needs no credentials, so a project is demonstrable before anyone has a key.

nodes.label: make check / CI Parity
nodes.rationale: make check runs the same commands in the same order as ci.yml; a local check that passes while CI fails is worse than no local check at all.

nodes.label: Tool Config Lives in pyproject.toml
nodes.rationale: pytest, ruff and mypy only auto-discover config at the project root; moving it to a config/ directory means every invocation needs explicit flags, and the day one gets forgotten the tool runs with different settings than CI.

nodes.label: Coverage Gate Starts at 70%
nodes.rationale: A gate you cannot meet gets deleted; a gate slightly above where you are gets met. Raise it as the project earns it.

nodes.label: Reuse the Cockpit Frameworks
nodes.rationale: Rather than reimplementing PII masking, prompt-injection detection, cost tracking, RBAC or audit logging, pull them from AI_Engineering_Cockpit.
